title: 2 Kings 1:1–8
context: After the death of Ahab, Moab rebels against Israel. Ahaziah, king in Samaria, falls through the lattice in his upper room and is sick. He sends messengers to “inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron,” whether he will recover from this sickness. The name is given as the WEB has it, Baal Zebub, a Philistine god at Ekron; the sense of the name is discussed and need not be settled here. The LORD’s angel sends Elijah the Tishbite to meet the messengers with a question that will be repeated: is it because there is no God in Israel that they go to inquire of Baal Zebub? Therefore, the LORD says, Ahaziah will not come down from the bed where he has gone up, but will surely die. Elijah departs. The messengers return at once; Ahaziah asks why, and they report the man’s word, including the sentence of death. When the king asks what kind of man he was, they answer, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” Ahaziah says, “It’s Elijah the Tishbite.” Both traditions read the unit as a turn away from the God of Israel to a foreign god, and as a word from the LORD that meets that inquiry before it reaches Ekron. The offense is the one the angel and the prophet name. No party fork is required.

verses.text: Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.
verses.arminianNotes:
The new book opens with a political fact: “Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.” The revolt is dated to the vacancy left by Ahab, and the verse does not yet name Ahaziah or the sickness that will follow.

Arminian readers hear a real shift in the region after a king’s death. Moab’s rebellion is a human act, set down as history, not as a symbol of the inquiry that is about to come.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the line as a dated notice at the book’s start. After Ahab’s death, Moab rebels against Israel.

Both traditions let the verse stand as the opening setting. The next verses will turn to the king in Samaria, without this revolt being forced into a type.

verses.text: Ahaziah fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick. So he sent messengers, and said to them, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this sickness.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahaziah “fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick.” He sends messengers and says, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this sickness.” The fall is accidental as far as the report goes; the inquiry is a chosen turn to a Philistine god.

Arminian readers hear a free and grave decision. The king might have asked the LORD; he sends instead to Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, to learn whether he will recover.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also distinguish the fall from the sending. The lattice and the sickness set the occasion; the word he speaks is an inquiry of Baal Zebub, not of the God of Israel.

Both traditions take that inquiry as the offense the following word will name. The god is identified as the god of Ekron; further claims about the name should remain modest.

verses.text: But the LORD’s angel said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and tell them, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s angel said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria,” and tell them, “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?” The speech continues into the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a real sending and a real question. The angel does not wait for the messengers to reach Ekron; Elijah is to meet them with this charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the word comes from the LORD’s angel to Elijah, and that the question assumes what Israel should already know: there is a God in Israel.

Both traditions take the verse as the LORD’s initiative against the inquiry, not as Elijah inventing a message of his own.

verses.text: Now therefore the LORD says, “You will not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but you will surely die.” ’ ” Then Elijah departed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The word is completed: “You will not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but you will surely die.” Then Elijah departed. The sentence is certain, and the prophet leaves once it is spoken.

Arminian readers hear a declared end, not a piece of advice. Ahaziah will not come down from that bed, and he will surely die. The king’s inquiry has been answered by the LORD, not by Baal Zebub.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the wording heavy. “you will surely die.” is the LORD’s word, and Elijah departs, his errand to the messengers done.

Both traditions receive the sentence as the heart of the unit. The messengers will now carry it back, and the king will later hear it from Elijah himself.

verses.text: The messengers returned to him, and he said to them, “Why is it that you have returned?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The messengers returned to him, and he said to them, “Why is it that you have returned?” They have not had time, in the story’s terms, to complete a journey to Ekron. The king notices the early return and asks why.

Arminian readers hear a genuine question. Ahaziah expected a trip to Ekron, and the swift return has to be explained.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the question at face value. The messengers are back, and the king wants to know why.

Both traditions read the verse as the hinge between Elijah’s meeting and the report that follows. The reason will be given in their next speech.

verses.text: They said to him, “A man came up to meet us, and said to us, ‘Go, return to the king who sent you, and tell him, “The LORD says, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel that you send to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you will not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but you will surely die.’ ” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
They report that a man came up to meet them and sent them back with the LORD’s word: the same question about God in Israel and Baal Zebub, and the same sentence, “you will not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but you will surely die.” The message has reached the king through his own messengers.

Arminian readers hear the word faithfully passed on. They do not yet name the man, but they do not alter the sentence they were given.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD’s saying, already spoken by Elijah, now stands in the king’s hearing in the same terms.

Both traditions take the report as an accurate carrying of verses 3–4. The king has the word; he still does not have the prophet’s name.

verses.text: He said to them, “What kind of man was he who came up to meet you and told you these words?”
verses.arminianNotes:
He said to them, “What kind of man was he who came up to meet you and told you these words?” Ahaziah asks after the messenger, not after a way to repent of the inquiry already named.

Arminian readers hear a question about identity. The king wants to know what kind of man spoke this word, and the next verse will give him an answer he recognizes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to load the question with a change of heart the text does not state. He asks what kind of man it was who told them these words.

Both traditions let the inquiry stand as a request for a description, which the messengers are about to supply.

verses.text: They answered him, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It’s Elijah the Tishbite.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They answered, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It’s Elijah the Tishbite.” The description is enough. Ahaziah names the prophet at once.

Arminian readers hear recognition, not a first introduction. The king knows Elijah from the last reign, and the hairy man with a leather belt is, for him, enough to say the name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same close. The messengers describe; the king identifies: “It’s Elijah the Tishbite.”

Both traditions end the unit on that identification. The word has been heard, the speaker is known, and the next passage will show what the king does with that knowledge.
